title: The Unworn Legs That Led to the Jaipur Foot
dek: In late-1960s Jaipur, a surgeon and a craftsman built a rubber foot for patients who went barefoot, squatted and sat cross-legged.

story.founder: P. K. Sethi and Ram Chandra Sharma
story.event: Designing a cheap rubber foot that let amputees squat, sit cross-legged and walk barefoot
story.summary: In the late 1960s at the Sawai Man Singh Medical College Hospital in Jaipur, orthopaedic surgeon P. K. Sethi found that amputees were abandoning artificial legs whose imported foot needed a shoe and stopped them squatting or sitting cross-legged. With the craftsman Ram Chandra Sharma, and a local tyre retreader who vulcanised the rubber, he developed the low-cost Jaipur Foot around 1968, presented it in 1970, and from 1975 a Jaipur charity paid for limbs for poor patients.
paragraphs: In the 1960s P. K. Sethi, who ran the orthopaedic department at the Sawai Man Singh Medical College Hospital in Jaipur, kept meeting amputees he had fitted with artificial legs who had stopped wearing them. The trouble, he came to see, was the foot. The standard imported design, the SACH foot developed at Berkeley in 1957, needed a shoe, and its wooden keel kept a wearer from squatting or sitting cross-legged. Many of his patients were farmers who went barefoot, worked in wet fields and sat on the floor.

Sethi, a general surgeon, had been asked to start the department in 1958 because the national medical council required one. He set out what was needed: a foot that looked bare, was waterproof and durable, flexed on uneven ground, allowed squatting and sitting cross-legged, and was made of cheap materials found locally. His partner was Ram Chandra Sharma, a craftsman who had taught aluminium work at Jaipur's School of Art and Craft, and whom Sethi called "Masterji".

Using an old sand-casting method, Ram Chandra made a die for a natural-looking foot. Large manufacturers would not help, and Sethi, his obituary records, knew "next to nothing about rubber". So they turned to Chuga Bhai, who ran a one-man tyre-retreading shop near the hospital. The first vulcanised foot was too heavy. Modification followed modification until they dropped the imported assembly and replaced the rigid keel with rubber blocks that gave enough at the ankle to squat and twisted enough to sit cross-legged.

Sethi presented the foot to Indian surgeons in Bangalore in 1970, and that year to the British Orthopaedic Association in Oxford. Poor amputees began travelling to Jaipur, but even a cheap limb was beyond many. From 1975 a charity founded by D. R. Mehta, a civil servant, used money raised at a Jain festival to pay for limbs and train fares; the number helped rose from 59 that year to 2,035 in 1980. Accounts differ over who first had which idea, and the Science Museum in London notes that Ram Chandra received little credit, largely because of his low social status. Accepting a Magsaysay Award in 1981, Sethi said: "Instead of looking to the West for our inspiration, it enabled us to look to our poor peasant for his approval."

quote.text: The man who is an artist finds his artistic freedom when he finds his ideal of art. Then is he freed from laborious attempts at imitation, from the goadings of popular approbation.
quote.source_title: Sadhana: The Realisation of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #6842
quote.connection: Tagore says an artist becomes free once he finds his own ideal, released from imitation and from chasing applause. Sethi and Ram Chandra, who had taught at an art school, found theirs by measuring the foot against a farmer's day rather than a foreign catalogue.

reflection: This breakthrough began with something easy to miss: a leg left unworn. The patients were not being difficult. The device had been made for someone who wore shoes and sat on chairs, and they were saying so in the only way open to them.

You will meet the same signal in your own work: a form nobody fills in, a tool colleagues quietly route around, a routine built for someone else's day. It is tempting to read that as resistance. Often it is the most honest feedback you will get. And when the fix comes, it is worth remembering who held the hammer.
invitation: Find one thing at work that people quietly avoid using. Ask one of them, without defending it, what they do instead and why.

sources.title: The Jaipur Foot and the 'Jaipur Prosthesis' (Rakesh Bhargava)
sources.supports: The SACH foot developed at UC Berkeley in 1957; it needed a shoe and was rejected in barefoot, floor-sitting, wet-field farming cultures; its wooden keel prevented squatting and cross-legged sitting; replacing the keel with rubber allowed dorsiflexion for squatting and torsion for sitting cross-legged; Master Ram Chanderji taught aluminium work at the local School of Art and Craft before Sethi brought him to the rehabilitation centre; later controversy over whose concept the rubber block was.

sources.title: Sethi, Pramod Karan: 1981 Ramon Magsaysay Award for Community Leadership (citation and response)
sources.supports: Imported limbs needed shoes and were discarded because users could not sit cross-legged, squat or walk on uneven ground; farmers who traditionally go barefoot; Sethi asked in 1958 to organise an orthopaedic department required by the medical council; Ram Chandra's die made by an age-old sand-casting method; large manufacturers refused to help and a small tyre-retreading shop vulcanised the foot; from 1975 the Mahavir Society for the Physically Handicapped used money raised at a Jain festival to pay for limbs and railway tickets, helping 59 people in 1975 and 2,035 in 1980; Sethi's acceptance speech, including 'Instead of looking to the West for our inspiration, it enabled us to look to our poor peasant for his approval.'

cross_checks.claim: The Jaipur Foot was developed at SMS Medical College Hospital, Jaipur, around 1968, by P. K. Sethi and the craftsman Ram Chandra (Sharma).
Imported artificial feet needed shoes and prevented squatting and cross-legged sitting, so rural amputees abandoned them.
A small local tyre-retreading shop vulcanised the rubber foot in Ram Chandra's die after larger manufacturers would not help.
From 1975 a Jaipur charity (BMVSS) funded limbs for poor amputees.
Sethi received the Ramon Magsaysay Award in 1981.

research_notes: Credit is disputed and the story says so. The Science Museum says Ram Chandra Sharma approached Sethi with the idea, which he said came to him after a flat tyre while cycling; Sethi's obituary and the Magsaysay citation present Sethi as setting the problem and Ram Chandra as making the die; Bhargava (2019) describes a controversy over whose concept it was to replace the SACH foot's wooden keel with rubber; BMVSS's own site credits 'a group of eminent Orthopedic surgeons and highly innovative craftsmen' without naming them. The story names both men, attributes the flat-tyre claim only by saying 'accounts differ', and quotes the Science Museum on Ram Chandra's lack of credit. Names: he appears as Ram Chandra (obituary, Magsaysay), Ram Chandra Sharma (Science Museum) and Master Ram Chanderji (Bhargava); the slate's 'Ram Chandra Sharma' is kept. Date: BMVSS and the Science Museum give 1968; some secondary sources give 1969; Sethi first presented it in 1970. The story dates the problem to 'the 1960s' and the presentation to 1970. Cost: the Science Museum's figure of $45 is undated and not used; its claim that most contemporary prostheses were carbon fibre looks doubtful for 1968 and is not used. The charity: the Magsaysay citation calls it the Mahavir Society for the Physically Handicapped, the English rendering of Bhagwan Mahaveer Viklang Sahayata Samiti; the 59-to-2,035 figures are from the 1981 citation. Funding is set to 'public' because the 1968-70 development took place in a state medical college's rehabilitation unit; BMVSS, the charity, came in 1975. The obituary's phrase 'next to nothing about rubber' appears in quotation marks there and is attributed to the obituary. Design lineage: the obituary says the SACH foot assembly was eventually eliminated and different components used, while Bhargava (2019) calls the Jaipur Foot technically a modification of the SACH foot with its wooden keel replaced by rubber; the story says they dropped the imported assembly and replaced the rigid keel with rubber, which both accounts support. The PubMed Central pages load but the verifier does not match the combined founder string on them; four other sources load and name the founder or company.
